analytical_models.equation_role: Determine phase stability: the phase with lower Gibbs free energy is more stable at equilibrium; point A marks the composition where BCC and FCC have equal Gibbs energy.
analytical_models.model_name: Gibbs free energy model (BCC vs FCC)
analytical_models.model_note: At 500 °C, considering the elemental partitioning according to Fig. 4a-b and Table 1, the same Gibbs free energies are obtained for both ferrite and austenite (dashed line in Fig. 4c); Al content change does not remarkably influence phase stability, and Mn partitioning mainly dictates the Gibbs energy and phase stability.

Mn content at BCC/FCC intersection (point A) at 500 °C
Mn content in BCC (point C) at 500 °C
Mn content in FCC (point B) at 500 °C

computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: Fe-11.15Mn-5.6Al-0.07C (wt.%) system; equilibrium mass percentages of Mn and Al in constituent phases; isothermal Gibbs free energy of BCC and FCC versus %Mn (6-20) and %Al (2-10) at 500 and 550 °C
computational_details.simulation_method: CALPHAD thermodynamic modeling / Gibbs free energy model
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Predicted partitioning (Mn enriched in austenite, Al enriched in ferrite) is compared with the SEM-EDS composition analysis (Table 1); at 500 °C the partitioned compositions of BCC and FCC give exactly the same Gibbs energy, supporting the bidirectional transformation.

defect_interactions.interaction_type: intersection of primary and secondary slip traces
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Within ferrite, strain is accommodated by multiple slip systems {110}<111> and {112}<111>; primary and secondary {110} and {112} slip traces intersect at a single point, and the wavy character of dislocation movement with high dislocation maneuverability promotes dislocation cell/HDDW formation.

defect_interactions.interaction_type: strain-induced austenite-to-ferrite transformation as strain compensation
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: At the imposed strain of 0.3, fresh ferrite grains form within prior austenite islands; the deformation-induced austenite to ferrite transformation acts as a strain compensation mechanism and justifies the observed flow softening at this low temperature.

interfaces.phase_evolution: Strain-induced austenite to ferrite transformation: fresh ferrite grains form within the prior austenite at the imposed strain of 0.3, acting as a strain compensation mechanism.
interfaces.slip_behavior: Strain within ferrite is mainly accommodated by activation of multiple slip systems {110}<111> and {112}<111>; formation and intersection of slip bands is highly probable; a planar slip-like character starts to form; wavy dislocation movement and high dislocation maneuverability enable dislocation cell formation and HDDWs.

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Elimination of any probable segregation in the ESR material.
Hot rolled through 5 passes in the temperature range of 1100-1200 °C followed by air quenching.
Annealed at 950 °C for 1 h to attain a triplex (ferrite + austenite + martensite) microstructure; this is the parent process proc_annealed-950c-1h.
Specimen soaked 5 min at 500 °C before testing to reach thermal equilibrium condition.
Compression by Gotech AI-7000 universal testing machine with a programmable furnace at a strain rate of 0.001 s^-1; interrupted at true strain 0.3.
Immediately water quenched to preserve the deformed microstructure.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: interrupted at true strain 0.3; water quenched

defects.type: heavily deformed parent austenite (dislocation configuration different from ferrite at same strain)

phases_present.morphology: fresh ferrite grains formed within the parent austenite (strain-induced austenite-to-ferrite transformation)

structures.overall_structure: Triplex (ferrite-based) low density steel deformed in compression at 500 °C to interrupted true strain 0.3: ferrite accommodates strain through cell-structure formation and high dislocation density walls (HDDWs) with a starting planar slip-like character, and fresh ferrite grains form within prior austenite islands via strain-induced austenite-to-ferrite transformation; deformation bands begin to develop in ferrite.

unmapped_findings: The compressive true stress-strain curve of this material at 500 °C and 0.001 s^-1 peaks near the 550-560 MPa level and shows appreciable flow softening after a true strain of 0.3 (Fig. 1c); note the curve corresponds to the full compression test to true strain 0.6, of which the present sample is the interruption at ε=0.3.

The starting microstructure before deformation is a triplex (ferrite + austenite + thermally induced martensite) obtained by annealing at 950 °C/1 h, with extremely low dislocation density in the ferrite and austenite phases (Fig. 1a-b).

The SEM-EDS compositional partitioning reported in Table 1 (Mn 10.3±0.1 wt% in ferrite vs 12.8±0.1 wt% in austenite; Al 6.0±0.1 wt% in ferrite vs 4.7±0.1 wt% in austenite) is stated for deformation at 500 °C up to a true strain of 0.6, so it nominally belongs to the ε=0.6 sibling sample rather than this ε=0.3 sample.
The steel has a high stacking fault energy of 80-110 mJ/m^2, which makes the austenite-to-martensite transformation theoretically impossible and rules out a classical TRIP effect.

Deformation-induced ferrite transformation (DIFT) and deformation-induced austenite transformation (DIAT) occur simultaneously at 500 °C (a phenomenon only observed at this low temperature regime and not at 600 °C), acting as an effective strain compensation mechanism.
